title: Dimensional Modeling: Star Schemas & Slowly Changing Dimensions
summary: How Kimball-style star schemas split a business process into facts and dimensions, why the grain must be declared first, and how SCD Type 2 keeps history so last year's reports don't change when a customer moves.
takeaways: A star schema is one fact table of measurements surrounded by dimension tables of descriptive context.
Declare the grain before anything else. Every fact row must mean the same thing, like one order line.
Dimensions use warehouse-owned surrogate keys, so one natural key can have many historical versions.
SCD Type 2 closes the current row and inserts a new version. Old facts keep pointing at the old one.

steps.label: Read snapshot
steps.detail: Today's source rows, keyed by the natural key (customer_id).

steps.label: Find current row
steps.detail: Look up the dimension row WHERE customer_id = ? AND is_current = 1.

steps.label: Compare
steps.detail: No row means a new member. Same tracked attributes means do nothing.

steps.label: Close old version
steps.detail: On a change, set valid_to = as_of and is_current = 0. Never overwrite the values.

steps.label: Insert new version
steps.detail: A new surrogate key, valid_from = as_of, valid_to = 9999-12-31, is_current = 1.

terms.definition: Numeric measurements of a business process event (quantity, revenue), plus foreign keys to its dimensions.
The who, what, where and when context for facts: customers, products, dates.
The precise meaning of one fact row, such as one row per order line. Declared before choosing facts or dimensions.
A meaningless integer primary key assigned by the warehouse, independent of the source system's natural key.
Type 1 overwrites an attribute and loses history. Type 2 adds a new row with effective and expiration dates.
A dimension key with no table of its own, like an order number stored directly on the fact.
